user.claim: ACP approval model is risk-tier-based, set at Coworker config time (not per-action at runtime): Low auto-executes, Medium batches into one per-run approval, High always requires explicit individual sign-off and is never batched. Runtime confirmation of every action would stall scheduled workers and create alert fatigue.
Risk tier is a platform-declared property set per-action/script in the Script Repository and per-workflow-node in the Runbook — not user-overridable at runtime.

Approval delivery differs by invocation surface: real-time N-zo chat surfaces inline interactive cards; scheduled/background workers pause to 'Waiting for Approval' and notify via persistent dashboard badge, automatic email, and execution-log status. Notification defaults to the MSP Admin who configured the Coworker (configurable).

Approval timeout (default 24h, second reminder at 12h) cancels/skips the blocked step and NEVER auto-approves — a stalled run beats an unreviewed high-risk action. Medium-risk batch waiting 24h → Cancelled/Approval Timeout; high-risk waiting 24h → Skipped.

Approval model enforces the Manual → Assisted → Autonomous progression but does not decide when to promote — a separate Trust/Autonomy Promotion system governs promotion. Promotion is admin-initiated with a system recommendation, never automatic (TRADE-004).

Medium-risk batch approval is modeled on Claude's batch-approval pattern: reduce decisions without reducing awareness; default CTA 'Approve all', secondary 'Review individually' path that skips unapproved actions.
Runs completing with a mix of approved and skipped steps are logged as 'Completed — Partial' (not Failed); the Value Ledger records value only for completed successful steps (IC-2026-002).

Five approval-model design decisions remain open (OQ-001..005): technician vs Admin-only approval authority; whether authority cascades to end-customer admin in multi-tenant; whether low-risk steps continue while a medium batch pends; snooze option; optional four-eyes second-approver for high-risk.

Trust score combines five components: track record (success rate over time), risk classification, scope boundaries, escalation rules, and audit trail — the L4 'earned autonomy' model (human confirms → AI executes, human audits).

Three competing trust/autonomy mental models are being tested for earned autonomy (L4): track record ('handled 47 patches → promote'), graduated dial (manual/assisted/autonomous slider per task), scope guardrail (low auto / med approval / high manual). Ewan Cameron's hypothesis: one must win a 10-second comprehension test — this is an open research question.

An AI Coworker is the deployable unit of automation: it assembles one or more N-able AI Experts + a Runbook (MSP's actual SOP) + MSP-approved scripts + MCP connections + guardrails into a named agent with a job description, risk policy, schedule, and accountability trail.

Trust model starts conservative (Manual: human approves medium+high risk); admin can promote only after the Coworker demonstrates a qualifying track record. N-able ships default platform Coworkers covering top research-identified use cases; MSPs run immediately or clone and customize.

The ACP management plane is AI-operator-accessible from day one; Coworkers may be assembled with help from an AI (N-zo or Claude Code) but follow the same lifecycle and approval model as human-initiated creation.

22 partner interviews confirm MSP high-volume tasks (patching, alert triage, endpoint health, ticket resolution, compliance audits, QBRs) are scriptable but rarely fully automated — because scripts are risky without governance, expertise is unevenly distributed across technicians, and MSPs lack a trusted mechanism to encode SOPs into agents.

Three primary personas: MSP Admin (full CRUD, activate, promote autonomy), MSP Technician (run on-demand, approve within permission level, cannot modify), AI Operator (Claude Code/N-zo — drafts + proposes changesets, cannot activate or approve own changes).
Invariant: activation is always a separate, explicit human operation — any actor (human or AI) creating a Coworker/Runbook produces a Draft; deployment never auto-activates.
Invariant: an AI operator cannot grant itself additional permissions — it operates only within permissions delegated by the authorizing admin session (INV-RISK-004, security-tested).
Invariant: platform (N-able-owned) Coworkers and Runbooks are immutable to tenants — MSPs may only clone them; clones are tenant-owned and isolated (INV-PROD-002, 403 on tenant PUT/PATCH).

Success metrics for Coworker v1: builder completion ≥70%, median start-to-activation ≤15 min, ≥80% of active Coworkers with a successful run in first 7 days, approval-timeout rate <10% (MET-001..004).

AI Experts are the N-able-owned/authored/published reasoning layer: specialized agents with a narrow domain that MSPs discover and select when assembling a Coworker but cannot configure. An Expert is typically an MCP server with a domain-specific system prompt and bound tools; can both reason AND execute, but only within declared domain scope and configured risk ceiling. In v1 only N-able can author/publish Experts; MSP-authored custom Experts are out of scope.

Expert platform invariants: out-of-domain execution and risk-ceiling violations enforced at the invocation layer (not config); Expert actions flow through the same risk-tier batch approval as all other actions and do not bypass it.

Expert configs are immutable/versioned: active config never mutated in place, all updates produce a new version, prior versions preserved; configs are read-only to all tenants (no MSP may modify/clone/override prompt, scope, tool bindings, or risk ceiling).

Expert lifecycle is Draft → Active → Deprecated; a Coworker must not invoke a non-Active Expert, and Draft/Deprecated Experts are invisible to assembly and the runtime invocation API. New Expert versions must not break in-flight executions (pinned versions keep running).

Every Expert invocation/action must be recorded in the audit log, attributing action to Expert identity, version, context passed, output returned, and the Coworker run it belongs to; runtime invocation target is structured reasoning output in <500ms p95.

MSP onboarding is a hard design constraint: net-new MSP goes from ACP signup to a scheduled, running AI Coworker in under 20 minutes without contacting support; any step exceeding its time budget in testing must be simplified before launch.

user.claim: Onboarding is a seven-step linear wizard: account creation → PSA connection → Coworker selection → Coworker config → first run → approval moment → schedule set. The activated Coworker is Ticket Triage & Dispatch against the 10 most recent open tickets in one ConnectWise queue.

Onboarding culminates in a live medium-risk batch approval — the MSP sees a real dispatch recommendation, approves it, and watches ConnectWise update; framed as the product demonstrating its model, not a bureaucratic gate.

The PSA connection framework is PSA-agnostic at the UX layer: one connection object across PSAs, with PSA-specific credential labels surfaced conditionally; must be reusable for ConnectWise, Autotask, HaloPSA, and future PSAs without redesigning the step.

Onboarding hard rules: PSA connection must pass live validation before advancing past Step 2 (no speculative connections); first run capped at 10 tickets server-side (no UI override); conservative approval policy default and non-configurable during onboarding; schedule mandatory (no skip); email verification sent at account creation but must not block the wizard.

Onboarding success metrics: median account-creation-to-first-run ≤20 min; ≥80% wizard completion; PSA-step drop-off <15%; first-run success ≥95%; ≥60% return to run a second Coworker within 7 days; zero MSPs exit without a schedule.

Onboarding time-to-value goal (Teams framing): sign up, activate, and complete a real coworker ticket-triage run within 20 minutes — via sign-up without an N-able account (link later) plus a tutorial 'Customer' shipping a fake PSA MCP and generic starter coworkers/experts/runbooks that can be hidden once live.

Decision: Models and MCPs are pre-requisite connections for the whole ACP product (not per-artefact), so MCP config should be built and sequenced BEFORE coworkers, which feed into them alongside runbooks and experts.

Friction point: experts and coworkers won't work without a model set, raising whether Bedrock should be on by default so a user can start a coworker without first configuring a model provider (paying for outcomes + token usage).
BYOM risk question: allowing self-hosted bring-your-own-model could let people siphon off runbook info, prompts, and guardrails — is that an accepted risk?

Runbook is a governed execution contract: plain-language intent + policy rules + AI reasoning boundaries + approved reasoning paths + workflow references + escalation logic + handoff behavior. 'AI Coworkers think, Runbooks govern how thinking becomes action'; Runbooks are Coworker-invoked, text-first, composable, contain deterministic Workflows; active configs never mutated in place (each change is a new version) and unresolved/unapproved references block activation.

Runbook data model decision: introduced a hasDraft boolean and made 'inactive' the default state for new and cloned runbook families, so users can see draft/active status without opening the runbook; active/inactive gates whether a coworker can run with that family.

Management plane is API-first and exposed as an MCP server — the MCP server IS the canonical interface (no separate 'AI mode'); AI operators submit 'proposed changesets' (PR-style) that a human admin must approve, and can never self-activate or approve their own changes.

Ownership of AI-created objects belongs to the approving admin, not the AI ('authorship-on-behalf-of'); objects carry created_by/approved_by/on_behalf_of metadata and revert to tenant ownership if the admin leaves — authority stays human.

Agent taxonomy: AI Agent Experts (N-able first-party, fixed runbook), Approved Vendor Experts (third-party, certified, governed via management plane), and AI Coworkers (customer-assembled super-agents combining Experts + own runbooks + own MCP connections). Each deployment gets its own scoped Non-Human Identity (NHI); no shared service principal across customers; identity enforced at runtime not config time.

Proposed experience principle: always show consequence previews/forecasts before a coworker runs — how many devices it will impact, results of manual vs auto-execute, token cost — to build trust rather than asking users to trust blind; suggests explicit 'preview panes' in the UI.

QBR Analyst is the build-first AI coworker — most broadly demanded in the 8 blind interviews (4 of 8, ranked #1 three times), high-intensity (cumulative 31, avg 7.8), and tops BOTH ranking cuts (survey mean-rank 2.90 and cumulative). Consistency across cuts is the strongest signal. Small-n qual: directional, not projectable.
Incident Response RCA is the consistent #2 coworker (cumulative 26); wanted by every cyber-deep operator and tied to cyber-insurance policy requirements.

Ticket Triage & Dispatch posts the highest intensity of the field (avg 8.3, daily volume), cumulative demand #3 (25); differentiated wedge is the live-diagnostics layer, not classification which is table-stakes in the PSA.

Autonomy is universally gated by buyers: graduated control — read-only diagnostics first, write-with-approval next, full automation only after trust earned; governance and rollback named as price of entry.

Survey drag-rank priority (n=39) leads with QBR business reporting (avg 2.90), then Alert flood suppression (3.23), Incident Response RCA (4.00); MSP Benchmarking ranks last (6.46). Individual value ratings (1-5) top out at Env Health Monitor 3.59 and QBR Analyst 3.40; Employee On/Offboarding lowest at 2.94 — narrow spread, no runaway on absolute value.
Partner-conference survey: 119 total responses, 75% (27 of 36 answering the value question) see overall value in the agent concepts.
Interview panel split 4 Build-ACP / 4 Narrow-MVP / 0 Do-Not-Build across 8 demand-validation interviews (12-17 June 2026, via Guidepoint).

Survey theme: integration gaps are a blocker — agents must connect to the PSA/RMM partners actually use; HaloPSA cited specifically. Data trust is a prerequisite — objectors cite data-sovereignty and non-consent to AI accessing customer data; transparency about data handling essential.

13 of 17 UEM users are concerned about agentic workflows, most commonly fearing AI 'going rogue', decisions made on inaccurate data, and unacceptable customer risk. Every one of the 17 expects human control and human approval regardless of comfort level.
Information gathering and troubleshooting are the top two roles users expect an AI coworker to play in UEM; these are also the most time-consuming everyday workflows.
AI assistance is seen as more valuable when embedded in-context (asset details panel) because the coworker already understands the working context — faster, more accurate responses.
A skeptical user (P17) moved from high concern to higher confidence over one session — agentic trust can be built incrementally with lower-adoption users.
A notable segment of MSP users do not use AI at all day-to-day, citing lack of interest, no time to think about implementation, and environmental concerns.

Users prefer AI in patch management as a supportive/assistive tool (reporting, diagnostics, recommendations) rather than fully autonomous patching; participants support automating responses to low-severity vulns and triggering actions (ticket, alert) when a vuln is actively exploited — tiered autonomy by risk.

Accountability is a core barrier: users ask 'who is responsible if AI declines a patch and a customer gets hacked?' and want clear audit trails plus human oversight. Users treat remediation as a governed process requiring risk decisions, accountability (who decided, when, why), and evidence — not a purely technical 'install a patch' action.

'Black box' behavior is a major blocker; users want verbose decision logs and transparency into how the AI reaches conclusions before trusting it. Users want source citations and data provenance on every answer (which system, filters applied, last-refreshed timestamp) to build trust and enable verification before client sharing.
Of 7 patch-survey respondents, all use N-central, all patch 300+ assets, and none currently use any AI in patching — a low adoption baseline for a coworker rollout.
'Human in the loop' was raised unprompted by multiple Empower customers — shared expectation that autonomous action is only viable after confidence is earned incrementally.

Without governance controls (ability to explicitly block remediation, prevent junior/automated override, record rationale), senior staff hesitate to grant access and features stay locked behind process, limiting adoption.
MSPs run data across four or more tools; N-zo's single-product scope limits value — users want the coworker to reach into COVE, SentinelOne, MSP Manager, MDR/EDR and billing for a unified assistant.
Engineers quickly distrust a tool that 'lies once'; N-zo returning incomplete/wrong data (e.g. 9 of 350 servers) erodes trust and discourages adoption.
Lack of chat history/session persistence was raised by almost every N-zo participant; losing conversation state on tab close drives 'one and done' behavior instead of sustained coworker use.

Users want a dedicated troubleshooting mode with structured outputs (symptoms, suspected causes, checks performed, findings, next actions) plus an evidence panel — shifting the coworker from 'doc search' to 'investigation assistant'.
Making clarifying questions the default when user intent is underspecified (client? site? date range? device group?) reduces wrong answers and speeds time-to-value.
Users requested a Developer/Automation entry point (API/MCP access with docs, keys, example workflows, guardrails) to build custom coworker workflows without cluttering the core UI.

User-reported time savings for N-zo (self-reported, not instrumented): QBR generation ~90 min → ~17.5 min (80.6%, 5.1x); root-cause/incident reporting 120 → 3 min (40x); resource-utilisation analysis 240 → 1 min (240x). An incident report was fully generated and exported to Word/PDF, letting a technician skip manual report-writing.

user.claim: Persona split is structural: technicians want raw data and lists; account managers/vCIOs want executive narratives translating stats into business value — one UI serving two audiences creates invisible friction.

Discoverability is a top UX blocker: Ask N-zo is buried on the asset tab, loses context on tab-switch, and has no chat history; partners want a standalone, bookmarkable app with persistent history — directly contradicting the headless aspiration.

Alert triage is a full-time human cost sink: a dedicated person spends ~20 hrs/week on alerts, 80-90% just checking — 'the output is mostly negative space' — making flood suppression/correlation a high-value target (UC-09).

License/cost reconciliation (active vs billed) is a near-universal MSP pain — 'ninety percent of the hands would go up' — but the data is not yet integrated; would-pay-if-ROI-clear signal (~$30/user) (UC-B).

Root-cause troubleshooting (UC-07) shows 100% adoption signal from one partner but is gated on missing data: limited historical (>24hr) data, missing events, network devices, last-logged-in user; '24 hours is nothing' for correlating 100 alerts.

Human-factors design imperatives (SDT / competence preservation): techs fear becoming button-pushers (if ACP shows WHAT not WHY, the senior tech is reduced to clicking approve — must surface reasoning); fear losing the next generation ('learned helplessness as a product side-effect', juniors never learn triage). Design must show WHY not just WHAT; the win is not 'saved 12 minutes' but 'Valentine's evening was free' (time returned to humans).
